sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext: "(Just Like) Starting Over" was the first single released from ''[[Double Fantasy]]'' and the first new recording Lennon had released since he left the music industry in 1975.<ref name=Listen177>{{cite book|last=Blaney|first=John|title=John Lennon: Listen to This Book|year=2005|publisher=Paper Jukebox|location=[S.l.]|isbn=978-0-9544528-1-0|edition=illustrated|page=177}}</ref> It was chosen by Lennon not because he felt it was the best track on the album, but because it was the most appropriate following his five-year absence from the recording industry. He referred to it during production as the "[[Elvis Presley|Elvis]]/[[Roy Orbison|Orbison]]" track, as he "tongue in cheek" impersonated their vocal styles. Lennon explained, "All through the taping of 'Starting Over,' I was calling what I was doing 'Elvis Orbison': '[[I Want You, I Need You, I Love You|I want you I need]] [[Only the Lonely|only the lonely]].' I'm a born-again rocker, I feel that refreshed, and I'm going right back to my roots."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.beatlesinterviews.org/db1980.1205.beatles.html|title=John Lennon - Rolling Stone Interview, 12/5/1980|date=1980|access-date=16 May 2023|archive-date=22 August 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240822000305/https://www.beatlesinterviews.org/db1980.1205.beatles.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> At the start of the [[Double Fantasy#2010 Stripped Down mixes|2010 "Stripped Down"]] version of the song, Lennon says "this one's for [[Gene Vincent|Gene]], and [[Eddie Cochran|Eddie]], and [[Elvis Presley|Elvis]]... and [[Buddy Holly|Buddy]]."
sections.text: "(Just Like) Starting Over" was the first single released from Double Fantasy and the first new recording Lennon had released since he left the music industry in 1975. It was chosen by Lennon not because he felt it was the best track on the album, but because it was the most appropriate following his five-year absence from the recording industry. He referred to it during production as the "Elvis/Orbison" track, as he "tongue in cheek" impersonated their vocal styles. Lennon explained, "All through the taping of 'Starting Over,' I was calling what I was doing 'Elvis Orbison': 'I want you I need only the lonely.' I'm a born-again rocker, I feel that refreshed, and I'm going right back to my roots." At the start of the 2010 "Stripped Down" version of the song, Lennon says "this one's for Gene, and Eddie, and Elvis... and Buddy."

sections.heading: Composition
Recording
sections.wikitext: Lennon recorded "(Just Like) Starting Over" on 9 August 1980 at [[The Hit Factory]]. The track was mixed at the [[Record Plant]] on 25–26 September 1980.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Madinger |first1=Chip |last2=Raile |first2=Scott |title=LENNONOLOGY Strange Days Indeed - A Scrapbook of Madness |year= 2015 |publisher= Chesterfield, MO: Open Your Books, LLC |pages= 520, 528 |isbn= 978-1-63110-175-5}}</ref>
sections.text: Lennon recorded "(Just Like) Starting Over" on 9 August 1980 at The Hit Factory. The track was mixed at the Record Plant on 25–26 September 1980.

sections.heading: Release and reception
sections.wikitext:
The song is Lennon's biggest solo hit in the US, staying at number 1 for five weeks. Before Lennon was murdered in New York City on 8 December 1980, the single had reached number 3 on the US charts. It reached number 1 for the week ending 27 December.<ref name=Listen177/> ''Billboard'' ranked it at the No. 4 song for 1981.<ref>[[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1981]]</ref> The song also reached number 1 on the ''[[Cashbox (magazine)|Cashbox]]'' Top 100.<ref name=Listen326>{{cite book|last=Blaney|first=John|title=John Lennon: Listen to This Book|year=2005|publisher=Paper Jukebox|location=[S.l.]|isbn=978-0-9544528-1-0|edition=illustrated|page=326}}</ref>

In the UK, it had peaked at number 8 in the charts and had fallen to position number 21 before [[Murder of John Lennon|Lennon's murder]] propelled it to number 1.<ref name=Listen177/> It was overtaken to the [[List of UK singles chart Christmas number ones|Christmas Number One Single]] rank by the [[St Winifred's School Choir]]'s "[[There's No One Quite Like Grandma]]," finishing at [[List of UK singles chart Christmas number twos|number 2]] on that list. This was particularly polarising as Lennon had been murdered three weeks prior. After two weeks at number one, a previous Lennon song, "[[Imagine (John Lennon song)|Imagine]]", replaced it.<ref name=notquite>{{Cite journal |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/music/features/not-quite-top-of-the-pops-stuck-at-number-two-for-christmas-1845917.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220501/https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/music/features/not-quite-top-of-the-pops-stuck-at-number-two-for-christmas-1845917.html |archive-date=1 May 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=Not quite Top of the Pops: Stuck at Number Two for Christmas |author =Andrew Johnson |author2 =Claire Cooper |author3 =Victoria Richards |date=20 December 2009 |journal=The Independent on Sunday }}{{cbignore}}</ref> By 6 January 1981, there were three Lennon songs in the UK top 5, a feat that remained unequalled for 35 years until [[Justin Bieber]] accomplished this in January 2016.

''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine considered "(Just Like) Starting Over" to be an "uptempo, fresh sounding rocker," praising the "irresistible melody and lyric line," the "exceptional rhythm unit" as well as Lennon's vocal performance.<ref>{{cite news|title=Top Single Picks|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=November 1, 1980|page=91|accessdate=2020-07-08|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-Billboard/80s/1980/BB-1980-11-01.pdf}}</ref>  ''[[Record World]]'' said that "John steps briskly into the mainstream with this glorious pop-rocker."<ref name=rw>{{cite magazine|magazine=[[Record World]]|date=November 1, 1980|page=1|accessdate=2023-02-22|title=Hits of the Week|url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Record-World/80s/80/RW-1980-11-01.pdf}}</ref>

In 2013, ''Billboard'' ranked it as the 62nd biggest hit of all time on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] chart.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=http://www.billboard.com/articles/list/2155531/the-hot-100-all-time-top-songs?list_page=4 |title= Hot 100 55th Anniversary: The All-Time Top 100 Songs |magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |date= 2 August 2013 |accessdate= 9 August 2013 |first= Fred |last= Bronson}}</ref>

''[[Stereogum]]'' contributors Timothy and Elizabeth Bracy rated it as Lennon's seventh best solo song, saying that it "finds him in throwback mode, delightfully evoking the [[doo-wop]] of his childhood on an uncharacteristically winsome ode to rejuvenated love."<ref>{{cite web|title=The 10 Best John Lennon Songs|date=13 May 2014|last1=Bracy|first1=Timothy|last2=Bracy|first2=Elizabeth|accessdate=2023-05-03|publisher=[[Stereogum]]|url=https://www.stereogum.com/1681100/the-10-best-john-lennon-songs/lists/}}</ref> ''[[Ultimate Classic Rock]]'' critic Stephen Lewis rated it as Lennon's seventh greatest solo love song, saying that "The undeniably catchy rock and roll song – a tribute to past rock and rollers – appeals to ears and hearts, with a solid groove and an optimistic and wistful lyric that is honest, without becoming maudlin."<ref name=ucr>{{cite web|title=Top 10 John Lennon Love Songs|url=https://ultimateclassicrock.com/john-lennon-love-songs/|author=Lewis, Stephen|accessdate=2023-01-08|date=20 March 2013|publisher=[[Ultimate Classic Rock]]}}</ref>
sections.text:
The song is Lennon's biggest solo hit in the US, staying at number 1 for five weeks. Before Lennon was murdered in New York City on 8 December 1980, the single had reached number 3 on the US charts. It reached number 1 for the week ending 27 December. Billboard ranked it at the No. 4 song for 1981. The song also reached number 1 on the Cashbox Top 100.

In the UK, it had peaked at number 8 in the charts and had fallen to position number 21 before Lennon's murder propelled it to number 1. It was overtaken to the Christmas Number One Single rank by the St Winifred's School Choir's "There's No One Quite Like Grandma," finishing at number 2 on that list. This was particularly polarising as Lennon had been murdered three weeks prior. After two weeks at number one, a previous Lennon song, "Imagine", replaced it. By 6 January 1981, there were three Lennon songs in the UK top 5, a feat that remained unequalled for 35 years until Justin Bieber accomplished this in January 2016.

Billboard magazine considered "(Just Like) Starting Over" to be an "uptempo, fresh sounding rocker," praising the "irresistible melody and lyric line," the "exceptional rhythm unit" as well as Lennon's vocal performance.  Record World said that "John steps briskly into the mainstream with this glorious pop-rocker."

In 2013, Billboard ranked it as the 62nd biggest hit of all time on the Billboard Hot 100 chart.

Stereogum contributors Timothy and Elizabeth Bracy rated it as Lennon's seventh best solo song, saying that it "finds him in throwback mode, delightfully evoking the doo-wop of his childhood on an uncharacteristically winsome ode to rejuvenated love." Ultimate Classic Rock critic Stephen Lewis rated it as Lennon's seventh greatest solo love song, saying that "The undeniably catchy rock and roll song – a tribute to past rock and rollers – appeals to ears and hearts, with a solid groove and an optimistic and wistful lyric that is honest, without becoming maudlin."
